title: The Endless House
premise: Cyrus Fairweather hosts a late-night radio show from a rented house in the village of Hollowmere, where his callers are all people who died the previous week—yet they speak as if alive, and only he can hear them. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings across the village, Cyrus realizes the dead are not haunting him; they are rehearsing a hymn whose final verse, if sung by the living, will trade every villager's memory for one soul's survival. The song was written by his great-grandfather, who cheated a drowning in 1911 and left the debt to his bloodline. To end it, Cyrus must learn the last verse without ever singing along, confront the drowned congregation still waiting in the flooded quarry, and choose between erasing himself from all memory or letting the village pay. He sings the verse alone at dawn, unmaking himself—but the final chapter reveals a listener calling in to a radio show hosted by someone named Cyrus Fairweather, keeping the lights on.
about_author: Jude Thackeray is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent six years answering calls from strangers at 3 a.m. and never quite stopped wondering who was on the other end. The Endless House is their second novel, written in a rented cottage whose doors they counted nightly out of habit.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. We meet him mid-broadcast in the endless house, taking a call from Edith Marsh—who he knows died last Tuesday. He keeps his voice steady, logs the call, counts the doors: eleven inside, twelve outside. Emotional beat: controlled dread masked as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Listener Log
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. He reviews months of recordings and realizes every caller died within seven days of phoning, always mentioning the same lullaby-like hymn. His producer friend Nell visits and hears nothing on the tapes but static. Beat: isolation deepening; the horror is his alone.

chapters.title: Twelve Doors
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A thirteenth door appears overnight between the pantry and the stairs, painted wet. He nails it shut; by morning the nails are on the kitchen table, arranged like musical notes. Beat: the house itself is complicit.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Village POV shifting to Cyrus. The whole of Hollowmere hears the church bell at midnight—though parish records confirm it was melted down in 1911. Only Cyrus recognizes the bell's rhythm as the opening bars of the hymn. Beat: private haunting becomes public event.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Request
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Edith calls again, lucid, begging him to visit her grave before Sunday and warning: 'Don't learn the words.' At the churchyard he finds her headstone freshly inscribed with a date next week. Beat: grief braided with urgency.

chapters.title: Nell Hears Static
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell secretly records a night in the house and plays it back: beneath the static, forty voices singing in rounds. She says nothing to Cyrus, terrified of what admitting she heard it will cost her. Beat: the curse spreads through witness.

chapters.title: Parish Records, 1911
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. In the county archive he finds the truth: the bell was recast from scrap after the quarry flood drowned thirty-one congregants mid-hymn—including a Fairweather listed among survivors. Beat: the past reaches up and takes him by the throat.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, dream sequence bleeding into waking. He dreams of standing waist-deep in black water while a choir sings around him, each face turning when he hums along without meaning to. He wakes with water in his lungs and a verse stuck in his head. Beat: contamination—he already knows too much.

chapters.title: What Nell Buried
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell confesses she recorded the voices; that night her own mother called the show—died three years ago. She begs Cyrus to burn the station down. He refuses: the callers are his only witnesses now. Beat: alliance strained by fear.

chapters.title: The Great-Grandfather's Ledger
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. In the house's sealed cellar he finds his great-grandfather Ezra's ledger: a bargain written in hymnal notation—one life spared in 1911, payment deferred 'unto the third singer.' The endless house was built over the quarry's old pump-house. Beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: Sunday Service
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The village attends a service led by a vicar no one remembers hiring; the congregation sings the hymn's first two verses from memory they don't have. Cyrus alone stays silent, mouthing nothing, hands over ears. Beat: communal sleepwalking toward sacrifice.

chapters.title: Caller Number Thirty-One
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A new caller identifies himself as Thomas Reeve, drowned 1911, and offers Cyrus a deal: sing the last verse willingly and live; refuse and the village sings it for you. Cyrus asks what happens to the singers. Silence, then: 'You're asking the wrong survivor.' Beat: temptation made explicit.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Doors in the house begin vanishing—ten, nine, eight—and with each one, a villager forgets something small: a name, a road, their child's middle name. Nell maps the losses against the door count. Beat: dread becomes arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Face
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus confronts the stranger-vicar, who wears the face of every drowned congregant in turn. The vicar explains gently: the hymn must be completed by a living voice of Fairweather blood; the village is merely the choir being assembled. Beat: the antagonist clarifies the trap—there is no innocent exit.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus studies the ledger's notation, teaching himself the last verse silently, writing it in ink mixed with quarry water so the dead can hear him read it but he cannot be made to sing. Each silent rehearsal costs him a memory—his mother's voice goes first. Beat: the price of survival made literal and personal.

chapters.title: One Door Left
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Only the front door remains. Nell finds Cyrus has forgotten her name though she stands in front of him; she realizes he is spending himself deliberately and decides to stay the night regardless. Beat: love persisting through erasure; resolve hardens.

chapters.title: The Quarry at Low Water
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Guided by Edith's final call, Cyrus descends into the drained quarry where the 1911 congregation waits, preserved mid-hymn, mouths open. They do not threaten him—they wait, patient, for the verse to be finished either way. Beat: awe and pity; the dead are victims, not villains.

chapters.title: The Third Singer
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Thomas Reeve appears bodily, revealed as the first Fairweather's accomplice who arranged the bargain and has waited a century for a descendant. He offers to take Cyrus's place if Cyrus will simply hum the melody—just once. Beat: climax of temptation; Cyrus nearly falters.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, climax. At dawn in the bell-less tower, with the village assembling below singing verses one and two, Cyrus reads the final verse aloud in the dead's hearing without singing a note—the loophole Ezra's ledger implied but never stated. The bell rings once, cracks the air, and the choir below falls silent mid-word. Beat: triumph purchased with everything he remembers about himself.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unrecorded
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. The village wakes remembering nothing of the week; the vicar is gone; the quarry refills overnight. Nell finds Cyrus sitting in the dark house, alive but blank—no name, no past, humming nothing. She tells him who he was. Beat: tender devastation; survival's cost tallied.

chapters.title: The Man Who Keeps the Lights On
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, fragmentary. Cyrus rebuilds a small life from Nell's accounts, keeps the radio as a night-light, counts doors out of instinct rather than fear. One evening he feels an unfamiliar peace—and an unfamiliar absence, like a room where furniture used to be. Beat: quiet acceptance of a self that cannot be fully restored.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Epilogue, unnamed caller's POV. Late at night, a listener phones a late-night radio show and asks the host his name. 'Fairweather,' he says. 'Cyrus Fairweather.' Behind him, faintly, a bell that doesn't exist begins to ring. Beat: chilling circularity—the story ends where it began, and the debt may only be sleeping.
